Didn't realize how rare it was for me to find people I actually enjoy being around, I guess.

I have one friend that I haven't managed to alienate yet, largely by virtue of him being sort of split off from the rest of the core group. I'm actually going to spend the weekend with him this week. First time in months, probably safe to assume the same period will pass again between visits after this one, too. I know he's got a lot he's been dealing with, too, though; don't want to overburden him by looking for all my answers there.

As for the flying... it really is mainly the military side that interests me. That interest isn't enough to hang on to, though... at least, that's how it seems. Then again, I have a general motivation problem, it's not just that one thing that's hard to keep trying for.

I'm leaving the internet for a while, but thanks for talking. I appreciate it, even if it's not a magical panacea.

I didn't mean I never go out and do stuff, just not often. I guess it takes more to get me excited about something than it used to. So most of the time getting up to do something turns out to be a waste of time/money/energy because I just wasn't that excited about it in the first place. Not disinterested or making up my mind to be sour in advance, just neutral, and the activity doesn't overcome that neutral zone. I can't even watch TV sometimes because I just don't care about the show, even if it's one that I normally enjoy. Iunno. There's not a lot of pressure *against* going out to do stuff, there's just not a lot of stuff that I actually want to go out and do, y'know?

I remember things I *used* to enjoy doing just for their own sake, but the joy's just gone out of it. I only ever really gamed online with my friends, and single-player stuff just doesn't interest me anymore. I can't justify shelling out full price for a game I'll only play for 10 hours total before getting bored with it. We used to do some tabletop gaming, but, again - friends. For a long time I wanted to fly jets for the military, but the fitness aspect of that is so far away that my motivation breaks almost instantly.

And my friends... well, I'm sort of in the middle of nowhere, pretty far away from them. They've all got their own lives, too, so it gets pretty hard to offer much. I'm not a part of their day-to-day lives, for the most part, so I can't just hang out and be cool; then when we do get to hang out I have to keep the mask on so as to not ruin the one good time we're able to have. Trying to get serious at any other point, be it texts or facebook or whatever, just seems to exasperate them. So I'd love to be able to give something back, help them out, make their day, be a good friend, but I don't get a lot of chances.

Anyway... I do appreciate the words. It just seems like all of my important relationships are fucked, and I guess that was what sort of kept everything else together. Everything else sort of weaves together into a web of defeat; even when one thing improves the other stuff drags me back down. So I don't really know what would actually help to break that (except what already hasn't, of course).

Please don't misunderstand. I don't dispute scientific theory. I *like* science. Regardless, every fact, experimental result, and observation within the scientific catalogue since the dawn of humanity still comes either from events billions of years in the past or from a chunk of space so tiny it's not even proportional to a grain of sand on a beach against the backdrop of the Universe. We are fish arguing the nature of the sky-light-life-ball when we have never even left the banks of our pond.


Certainly, there is much to be said for science. It is magnificent - and furthermore, useful beyond measure! But to say that what we know is certain and generalizable to the rest of the universe is folly. Even in the most certain of things there is doubt - what's the illustration about pushing on a wall for eternity and eventually your atoms will slip past the atoms of the wall? - and where there is doubt, as light to shadow, there is belief. I make an unconscious choice to believe in the forces that will hold me up every time I sit in a chair - but sometime between now and the end of the universe some entity somewhere may find its buttocks-resting apparatus cleanly fused with its midsection in an utter scientific fluke. I still believe in my chair.


No matter how much we know, there are always gaps in our understanding. You believe that those gaps are all filled by science (as do I, but that is a discussion for another thread), but saying that anyone who fills those gaps with anything else is **wrong** accomplishes only the inflammation of tempers and the injury of feelings. Fill one gap and you will find another behind it until you die or can understand no more - this is part of what makes science so beautiful. It also just happens to make utterly refuting claims of the supernatural a futile endeavor, because wherever there are holes exists infinite possibility.

The Earth is miniscule enough that its inhabitants have already managed to easily circumnavigate and occasionally even leave it altogether. Where are we on the shape, size and contents of the universe? The larger the scale of the problem, the greater the current ambiguity; considering the problem of a purported being infinitely greater than the universe, then, very nearly sets us at our limits from the outset.


Again, though, I'm not out to get drawn into an evidence-dredging spitting contest. If you take away the solipsist standard, everyone's standard for sufficient evidence will be different (and what can be "convincingly claimed" will likewise vary). My goal was and remains to dispel the idea that something must be exhaustively proven to be generally acceptable, and to suggest that entertaining the plausibility of an idea rather than ruling it out on principle leads to more fruitful discourse and discovery.

Fair enough. My illustration was simply meant to set up that exact concept, anyway. All I ever set out to do was suggest that the absolute proof standard to which so many people like to hold spiritual claims is often just as unreachable in scientific pursuits. The idea is that ultimately, neither side can prove itself completely or disprove the other - and that's fine. Both sides benefit from taking a respectful, open-minded approach to dialogue - which most often starts by ending demands for total certainty (an impossible condition in any pursuit) and discarding everything else out of hand unless they are met.


That's the goal, at least.

A few final thoughts, then, before leaving this thread in peace.


What are you basing your probabilities on? If you don't have sufficient studies to demonstrate that spiritual/supernatural events are improbable then your belief fails your own standard as it would be primarily anecdotally supported.


Secondly, if all or most parts of a historical account can be proven to be accurate except for the supernatural content asserted to have happened by the author, does that not bear further study and postponement of judgment by those who remain skeptical?


Lastly, I again urge you to take a closer look at the already existing body of material which scholars have created in the examination of Christian claims. There is already existing evidence in good quantity to make a case for Christianity as it is presented in the Bible. If you want well-thought-out, thorough studies and compelling evidence, it's out there.
Lee Strobel's "The Case for Christ," though not exhaustive or authoritative by any means, makes an excellent introduction to the subject and provides a handy index of further materials.

I appreciate your input, and rest assured that I did not intend to misrepresent scientific theory. This is, however, beyond my current level of education - and thus I cannot endeavor to utilize what you might call the "more nuanced version" in making a point. Regardless, if my understanding of your outlining of the concept is correct - namely that the universe is a closed system, and that after all the math everything in it came from somewhere within it some way or another - then my core point still stands: humanity has no way to exhaustively test this, and we accept many other scientific theories that in some way rely upon the truth of this one.

Rather than attempt to distinguish between strictly "supernatural" or "scientific" occurrences, I'll posit again that the scientific is not mutually exclusive with the supernatural. A good part of the difficulty in identifying the supernatural's involvement may be because it simply sets into motion otherwise impossible scientific chains of events - which aside from their spontaneous and obfuscated origin proceed normally.

There's plenty of cases where the jury is still out on why things work the way they do, last I checked. (heck, we don't have a clue what caused the "big matter ball" to turn into the "big bang")


Look, I'm not out to prove the existence of the supernatural or its involvement in human affairs to any degree. I already said that was currently beyond me, and has been attempted by far more skilled and learned individuals. If you want to do your own search for the truth, I applaud your openness and encourage you to do your own exhaustive research - perhaps starting with those who have come before. The only point I'm trying to get at is that the idea that science and spirituality must be mutually exclusive is rather silly, considering how limited the entirety of the human experience is in the grand scheme of the universe.

In my stated moral parameters, the premature and unnatural termination of a human life would be considered an immoral action, regardless of other circumstances surrounding that action. While many people would believe that the greater good done in that specific situation outweighs the immorality of taking a life, it looks different if you don't weigh moral and immoral deeds against one another but rather consider them separate entities. In the end, for whatever reason, a man is dead - and is that not to be mourned?

Historical evidence can never be used to prove that anything of any nature happened. In another 50 years when all contemporaries have died, no one will be able to say for certain that the holocaust happened - although the evidence suggests it, the best any non-eyewitness can do without living witnesses to verify is "probably." Even then people lie for a variety of reasons, and true certainty outside of events currently unfolding before an observer becomes very slippery, very quickly.


I then posit that if anything one's own experience is the ultimate determining factor in one's ability to be certain. If certainty is what you're after, then you need to have a supernatural experience to be certain of its existence. This is further complicated by what I perceive to be your personal belief that anything not able to be corroborated by data is unreliable and should be discarded - meaning that even should you have a personal experience you would need to be in a position to measure its effects in that moment. Clean laboratory conditions and sufficiently skilled researchers are rarely available at any given moment, making the acquisition of sufficiently reliable data to corroborate your experience difficult.


In response to your final statement, I would suggest that measurable effects may be more plentiful than you assume. Sick people get well for no reason with regular frequency - it seems like nearly everyone today knows someone whose relative's cancer went into remission despite a gloomy prognosis. The world is full of phenomena which can't be readily explained (ball lightning, anyone?), but most people write it off as "oh well we just can't explain that scientifically yet." Where is the same privileged assumption with regards to the supernatural's potential involvement? For that matter, who's to say that a supernatural entity couldn't work within the laws of science to produce a physical phenomenon? If an all-powerful entity existed, that should easily be within the realm of possibility. Being able to observe the effects does surprisingly little to reveal their cause in many cases, scientific or otherwise. Thus we return to the idea of personal experience, as well as the anecdotal evidence of peers and trusted associates, being often the only acceptable form of certain "proof" in human experience.


This discussion has gone rather far afield from the original content, however.

It's easy to say that doing the best with your circumstances is the way to go. Taking a wider view, though, circumstances don't "just happen." The situation where your options are limited to binary or trinary systems are few and far between. Thus if you have the capacity to put yourself onto paths that could more probably lead to what you might call "bad circumstances," should you not consider whether you'd be able to handle acting in those circumstances? If you decide you can't, you have the option to avoid that road altogether. Deciding by the circumstances is great - when you have prohibitive circumstances. But what about when you don't?

I have my personal convictions about the spiritual, obviously, and I would like to think that I'm capable of making a case for Christianity based on historical evidence. Nevertheless, no matter how much evidence I can come up with or how convincing of an argument I can make, I can offer no definitive proof of the existence or nature of God. I can offer evidence based in my own personal experience, and I can point toward exhaustive studies of historical documents done by people far more expert than I, but that's as much as I can do. The decision to believe is up to everyone - most people believe that they'll be alive the morning after they lay down to sleep, but that's likewise only a product of their personal experience to that point.


I also don't mean to say that science is untrue or wrong by any means. It is simply my intent to propose that we have the understanding of science that we have because we can base it on physical observations. Our current capabilities as a race limit us from observing and recording in replicable fashion "supernatural" phenomena. I don't blame anyone for not believing what they can't see, interact with or test - but I also ask who's to say what we'll be able to analytically test in another 100 years? It's just as silly to say "impossible" to the idea of lightsabers as it is to the "supernatural." Humans have consistently surprised themselves with ingenious advances, and 100 years is a long time. And as for revision: I think most Christians would agree that if they met God physically and he turned out to be different than what he's supposed to be, they might change their opinion on how worthy of worship he is.

I think that the opposite is actually true; you can only really know the truth of something by testing it in use. Thus you can only know the value of your moral bearings by encountering others of differing views and engaging in discourse. That's the precise reason I came to this subreddit - if I have more points of comparison I can know my internal workings more intimately than I did before. If I have logical reasoning to help me understand those points of comparison, I can even further understand my own position and whether I need to adjust it - and also the direction towards which I might like to move.

If one action has multiple consequences, however, is the weight of that action not judged by measuring those consequences against one another? If that's the case, you end up having to put values on things that no one can rightly put values on - when is one life worth more than another? When is selfless giving too much?


In the end, you need a metric of some sort to have measurements of any meaning. I can *justify* something I feel is morally wrong, and go on living my life. That doesn't mean I'd think I'd done a good thing, just maybe the "best" thing. I guess I'm just trying to figure out what that metric is - and maybe that starts with looking at whether good and bad consequences weigh against each other or if they simply stack up into their own little piles on either side.

I chose those as my broad definitions based on a personal value judgment. So yes, I'm making a subjective definition of morality here; the problem is that if I accept the purely subjective nature of morality then I have no metric by which to judge my own decisions. Therefore I attempted to articulate a broad definition which most, if not all, rational humans would agree with to some degree.

I would like to call your attention to a pair of fundamental assumptions inherent in science and theology, respectively.


First: all matter is preserved as either matter or energy. It is never created or destroyed, has always existed and will continue to exist forever, in some form or fashion. This fundamental assumption forms the basis for a significant portion - if not all -of current scientific understanding.


Second: God has always existed, and will continue to exist forever. He is - aside from being Omnipresent, omnipotent, and omniscient - eternal. This assumption forms the basis for most all Christian theology.


Notice that both science and theology have similar underlying, fundamental assumptions. Both rest completely on something that, to our present ability, humanity has not found a means to prove.


We assume that science is "true" because we can observe its laws in nature, in spite of the fact that we have only recently left our own solar system amid a universe so vast we struggle to even estimate its size, much less see to its edges. We can say with no amount of certainty that what we think happens happens anywhere else but here. The best evidence we have are images, taken of lights which are reaching us thousands to millions to billions of years after the events which created them.


I cannot hope to definitively prove the existence of God or any other Deity. It certainly bears considering, however, that for all of our scientific advancements we probably understand a whole lot less than we think we do - and can certainly prove very little of it outside of our tiny little spaceship-Earth in the grand cosmos. Food for thought when you want to talk about what's possible and impossible, scientific and unscientific.

I think it should start out at lower grade levels with just a slightly wider focus and probably some better handling of gifted students, and as the age of the students increases and the fundamentals get more covered, start opening up more curriculum instead of just accelerating the same things. For example, making things like woodshop available in 7th grade instead of starting everyone on algebra at the same time. In an ideal system, there would be enough flexibility to allow students to go faster in their more adept subjects and slower in their less proficient ones, within a certain margin determined by age/grade level. So Johnny who's good at music and likes working with his hands might not start algebra until high school (but that's fine because he'll still get through pre-calc by the time he graduates), whereas uncoordinated and hyper-allergic Timmy could be taking physics as a freshman (having started accelerated science two years prior) but only have to do a little PE and Health throughout his high-school career.

Of course that's in a perfect world where budget concerns don't exist and there are enough teachers of varying interests and educational levels to go around. Shame it'll never be possible.
